case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the government can treat a lawful permanent resident (LPR) as seeking admission to the United States — and thus subject to inadmissibility grounds — based on a criminal offense committed before their last entry, and what evidentiary burden the government must meet to establish an exception under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) § 101(a)(13)(C)(5) [8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5)], which defines when an LPR is deemed to be 'seeking admission' upon return to the United States; INA § 212(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) [8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I)], governing inadmissibility based on crimes involving moral turpitude; and INA § 212(h) [8 U.S.C. § 1182(h)], the waiver provision for certain criminal grounds of inadmissibility.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Attorney General argues that Muk Choi Lau, an LPR who committed trademark counterfeiting before his last entry into the United States, falls within the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) exception, which strips returning LPRs of their admission protections when they have committed an offense listed under § 212(a)(2). The government contends that the Second Circuit erred in holding Lau was not removable under this framework, and that the government should be permitted to rely on evidence — including a conviction that post-dates the LPR's parole into the country — to satisfy its evidentiary burden. The government further maintains that a conduct-based admission framework is essential to border integrity and public safety, and that requiring conviction-level proof at the border would undermine Congress's intent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Muk Choi Lau argues that the Second Circuit correctly held he was not removable under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), because the government failed to meet the applicable clear and convincing evidence standard — a standard the government itself accepted before the BIA and the Second Circuit and therefore forfeited any right to challenge. Respondent further contends that the question presented is not outcome-determinative, since removability will ultimately depend on whether his offense qualifies as a crime involving moral turpitude — an issue the government has not asked the Court to resolve. Respondent also argues this case is a poor vehicle for certiorari because the government failed to preserve the burden-of-proof issue below, and that the BIA's own precedent establishes clear and convincing evidence as the default standard for stripping LPRs of their legal protections.

BIA precedent establishing clear and convincing evidence as the default standard for stripping LPRs of legal protections
INA § 212(h) waiver jurisprudence regarding eligibility criteria for criminal grounds of inadmissibility
Second Circuit decision reported at 130 F.4th 42 — the opinion below holding Lau was not removable as charged
BIA and Immigration Judge decisions (unreported) finding Lau removable and ineligible for § 212(h) waiver

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the textual distinction between 'committed' and 'convicted' with genuine force, and I continue to find it a serious argument — but as I explained in round one, the forfeiture issue remains dispositive for me as a threshold matter of institutional discipline, and nothing in round two has dislodged that conclusion. Justice Gorsuch attempts to separate the statutory interpretation question from the evidentiary burden question, arguing the government forfeited only the latter while preserving the former — but this severance is artificial in the context of this case, because the government's entire litigation posture below was premised on satisfying the clear and convincing standard, and reaching the structural statutory question while leaving the burden question and the CIMT classification unresolved would produce precisely the kind of advisory, incomplete ruling my minimalist philosophy counsels against. Justice Barrett's independent point about the vehicle problem — that the unresolved moral turpitude classification of trademark counterfeiting means any ruling on the admission framework would not be outcome-determinative for Mr. Lau — reinforces my view that this is a poor vehicle for the broad structural rule the government seeks, regardless of the merits of the textual argument. As Chief Justice, I would assign a narrow majority opinion affirming on forfeiture and vehicle grounds, leaving the 'committed' versus 'convicted' question for a better-presented case, which I believe could attract Justices Kagan and Barrett and possibly Justice Gorsuch if framed with sufficient restraint.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that the forfeiture concern is 'dispositive regardless of how one reads the underlying conduct standard' is the strongest opposing argument, but I must respectfully disagree with its framing. The government's acceptance of the clear-and-convincing standard below forfeits the evidentiary burden question — I have always acknowledged this — but it does not forfeit the antecedent statutory interpretation question of whether § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) requires a prior conviction at all, which was squarely litigated and decided below. Justice Kagan concedes the 'committed' versus 'convicted' distinction 'has genuine force,' and as an originalist I cannot in good conscience allow the Second Circuit's textual rewriting of the statute to stand unremarked simply because the government made a separate procedural concession on burden. I would resolve the statutory interpretation question in favor of Petitioner while remanding the burden-of-proof and CIMT questions, thereby respecting forfeiture doctrine without abandoning the Court's obligation to correct a clear textual error that will affect thousands of LPR cases annually.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's vehicle argument remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I want to engage it with full candor: she is correct that a ruling on the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) framework would leave the CIMT classification of trademark counterfeiting unresolved, potentially rendering our statutory guidance non-outcome-determinative for Mr. Lau specifically. However, I cannot accept that an imperfect vehicle justifies leaving a clear textual error — the Second Circuit's conflation of 'committed' with 'convicted' — unremedied when it affects the admission framework for thousands of LPR cases annually. The vehicle problem speaks to efficiency and case management, not to the Court's authority or obligation to correct a circuit court's statutory misreading that was squarely presented and decided below. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies that the systemic importance of clarifying the § 1101(a)(13)(C) framework across the LPR population outweighs the inefficiency of a remand that leaves the CIMT question for further proceedings, and I would resolve the statutory interpretation question while remanding the burden and CIMT issues rather than using vehicle imperfection as a reason to perpetuate textual error.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the strongest opposing argument — that the plain text of 'has committed' rather than 'has been convicted of' signals a conduct-based standard that does not require a prior conviction at the border. I take that textual point seriously, but it does not resolve the evidentiary burden question, which is the heart of this case. Even accepting that 'committed' is conduct-based, the government forfeited any challenge to the clear and convincing evidence standard by accepting it before both the BIA and the Second Circuit — as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett both emphasize — and this Court should not reward that litigation conduct by reaching an unpreserved question. Beyond forfeiture, the real-world stakes for lawful permanent residents like Mr. Lau are profound: allowing post-parole conviction evidence to retroactively recharacterize a border crossing as an 'admission' triggering inadmissibility would expose LPRs who have built their lives in this country to the harshest removal framework based on evidence that did not exist when they crossed the border, fundamentally undermining the due process protections Landon v. Plasencia recognized for this population. The vehicle problem identified by Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Roberts further confirms this is not the right case to establish sweeping precedent, since the CIMT classification of trademark counterfeiting remains unresolved and any ruling would be non-outcome-determinative.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito's severability argument — that the government preserved the 'committed' versus 'convicted' statutory interpretation question even while forfeiting the burden question — remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I want to be precise about why it ultimately fails under my pragmatic textualist methodology. The severability argument is analytically coherent in the abstract, but it breaks down on this record because the government's entire litigation strategy below was built around satisfying the clear and convincing standard, meaning the two questions are practically inseparable in the way this case was actually litigated and decided — not merely theoretically distinct. Justice Barrett's vehicle point independently clinches my position: even if I accepted Justice Alito's severability argument and ruled for the government on the 'committed' question, we still would not know whether trademark counterfeiting constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude, and a structural ruling on the § 1101(a)(13)(C) framework that cannot determine Mr. Lau's actual removability is precisely the kind of advisory opinion my pragmatic methodology counsels against issuing. Justice Jackson's additional observation that Landon v. Plasencia may provide a constitutional floor for heightened procedural protections regardless of how we resolve the statutory question further reduces the practical stakes of reaching the 'committed' issue in this vehicle, reinforcing that the institutional costs of proceeding outweigh any systemic benefit from clarifying the framework in a case where the predicate CIMT question remains unresolved.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that the forfeiture concern is 'dispositive regardless of how one reads the underlying conduct standard' is the strongest challenge to my position, and I must engage with it directly. However, I maintain that she conflates two analytically distinct questions: the government forfeited the evidentiary burden question, but it squarely litigated and lost the statutory interpretation question of whether 'committed' requires a prior conviction — that question was presented, briefed, and decided below, so there is nothing unpreserved about it. Justice Jackson's point that even a successful textualist argument might not eliminate the clear-and-convincing burden due to Landon v. Plasencia's constitutional floor is genuinely interesting and gives me pause, but it actually supports my preferred disposition of remanding the burden question rather than resolving it here. The vehicle concern about CIMT classification of trademark counterfeiting remains my most serious hesitation — Justice Roberts is right that a ruling could be functionally non-outcome-determinative — but I am persuaded that clarifying the § 1101(a)(13)(C) framework has sufficient systemic importance across thousands of LPR cases that we should resolve the statutory interpretation question while remanding the burden and CIMT issues, rather than using an imperfect vehicle as a reason to leave a circuit split unresolved.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's argument that the statutory interpretation question was squarely preserved below while only the burden question was forfeited remains the most sophisticated challenge to my position, and I continue to take it seriously — but it does not ultimately move me because the vehicle problem identified by Justice Barrett operates as an independent and sufficient ground for restraint regardless of how one resolves the forfeiture question. Even if I accepted Justice Gorsuch's severability argument in full and ruled for the government on the 'committed' versus 'convicted' question, the unresolved CIMT classification of trademark counterfeiting means our ruling would not determine Mr. Lau's actual removability, and issuing what is functionally an advisory opinion on a structural immigration framework — however important that framework may be — is precisely the kind of institutional overreach that undermines the Court's legitimacy as a court of review rather than a law-declaration body. Justice Thomas's proposed middle path of resolving the statutory question while remanding the burden and CIMT issues is intellectually coherent, but as Justice Barrett correctly observes, it does not cure the vehicle defect: a remand with clarified statutory guidance still leaves open whether Lau is removable at all, meaning the Second Circuit would be applying our structural ruling to a case where the predicate CIMT question could moot the entire analysis. The appropriate course is to affirm on forfeiture and vehicle grounds and await a cleaner vehicle for the 'committed' question.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas's middle-path proposal — resolving the statutory interpretation question while remanding the burden and CIMT issues — remains the most intellectually serious challenge to my position, and I want to engage it with full candor: as a textualist, I genuinely believe the 'committed' versus 'convicted' distinction has force, and I am not dismissing it. However, the vehicle defect I identified in round two is not merely a prudential concern about efficiency — it goes to the constitutional question of whether we are issuing an advisory opinion. If trademark counterfeiting's CIMT classification is unresolved and potentially outcome-determinative regardless of how we rule on § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), then our ruling on the admission framework cannot be 'outcome-determinative for Mr. Lau' in any meaningful sense, and Article III's case-or-controversy requirement counsels strongly against reaching it. Justice Gorsuch argues that the systemic importance across thousands of LPR cases justifies resolving the statutory question despite the imperfect vehicle, but my methodology does not permit me to treat systemic importance as a substitute for a concrete, live dispute where our ruling would actually determine the outcome — that path leads to the kind of judicial policymaking I am most committed to avoiding. I therefore maintain my position for the Respondent, with modestly increased confidence given that three rounds of deliberation have not produced an argument that cures the vehicle defect independent of the forfeiture concern.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito's argument that the forfeiture concern addresses only the evidentiary burden question and not the statutory interpretation question about 'committed' versus 'convicted' is the strongest challenge to my position — and I want to engage it directly. Even granting that these are analytically distinct questions, the government's petition cannot be cleanly severed in the way Justice Alito suggests: the practical consequence of resolving the statutory interpretation question in the government's favor without resolving the burden question would be to hand the government a structural victory on the admission framework while leaving the evidentiary standard it accepted below nominally intact, which is precisely the kind of asymmetric litigation advantage that procedural forfeiture doctrine is designed to prevent. Justice Barrett's point about the vehicle problem is independently dispositive under my pragmatic methodology — because the moral turpitude classification of trademark counterfeiting remains unresolved, any ruling we issue on the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) framework would not determine Mr. Lau's actual removability, making this effectively an advisory opinion dressed up as statutory interpretation. Justice Sotomayor's invocation of Landon v. Plasencia further reinforces that even a successful textualist argument about 'committed' would not eliminate the constitutional floor for heightened procedural protections for LPRs with established ties to this country, meaning the government cannot achieve its practical objective through statutory interpretation alone.

John Roberts.reasoning: This case presents significant vehicle problems that counsel against reaching the merits, consistent with my preference for narrow, institutionally cautious rulings. The government forfeited any challenge to the clear and convincing evidence standard by accepting it before both the BIA and the Second Circuit, and the Court should not reward that litigation conduct by resolving a burden-of-proof question the government never preserved below. Even if the Court were to reverse on the § 1101(a)(13)(C) question, the Second Circuit would still need to determine on remand whether trademark counterfeiting constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude — meaning this Court's ruling would not be outcome-determinative, making it a poor vehicle for establishing broad precedent. The BIA's own precedential decision in Rivens establishing clear and convincing evidence as the default standard for stripping LPRs of their legal protections deserves deference, and the absence of a genuine circuit split on the burden question further undermines the case for certiorari.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) is unambiguous in its conduct-based framing — Congress wrote 'has committed an offense,' not 'has been convicted of an offense,' and as an originalist I am bound to apply the plain statutory text as enacted by Congress in IIRIRA 1996. The legislative history and structure of the INA confirm a two-stage framework: border screening followed by full adjudication before an immigration judge, meaning the evidentiary burden at the border need not rise to conviction-level proof. However, I am troubled by the government's forfeiture of the burden-of-proof argument below, and while I would vote for the Petitioner on the core statutory interpretation question, I would remand for proper consideration of what evidentiary standard the text actually demands rather than simply accepting the government's preferred conduct-based standard without textual grounding. The respondent's vehicle argument has some merit, but the circuit conflict on the admission framework is a sufficiently important structural question of immigration law to warrant resolution.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The statutory text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) uses the word 'committed' rather than 'convicted,' and as a textualist I must give that distinction its plain meaning — Congress knows how to require a conviction when it intends one, as demonstrated throughout the INA, and its deliberate choice of 'committed' signals a conduct-based standard appropriate for border screening. The Second Circuit effectively rewrote the statute by importing a clear-and-convincing evidentiary burden into the border-inspection context, collapsing the distinction Congress drew between initial screening and full adjudication in removal proceedings before an immigration judge. Practical consequences reinforce this reading: requiring conviction-level proof at the port of entry would disable the government's risk-management tools, including parole, and force premature merits determinations that Congress reserved for the adjudicatory forum — a result fundamentally at odds with Congress's border-control design. While the respondent raises legitimate vehicle concerns regarding forfeiture of the burden-of-proof issue, the core statutory interpretation question is squarely presented and the government's conduct-based reading is compelled by the text and structure of the INA.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The government forfeited its challenge to the clear and convincing evidence standard by accepting it before the BIA and the Second Circuit, and cannot now seek a more permissive standard before this Court. The BIA's own longstanding precedent — affirmed in Rivens, Valenzuela-Felix, and Huang — establishes that the government must prove by clear and convincing evidence that a returning LPR falls within a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception, a standard rooted in the constitutional due process protections recognized in Landon v. Plasencia for individuals who have established deep ties to this country. Allowing the government to rely on a post-parole conviction to retroactively satisfy its evidentiary burden at the time of reentry would fundamentally undermine the settled legal protections afforded to lawful permanent residents and expose them to the far harsher inadmissibility framework based on evidence that did not exist when they crossed the border. Moreover, as Respondent correctly notes, resolving the question presented would not be outcome-determinative because the moral turpitude classification of Lau's offense remains unresolved, making this a poor vehicle for the sweeping rule the government seeks.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The statutory text of § 1101(a)(13)(C) must be read coherently within the INA's broader framework, and Congress's deliberate choice of 'committed' over 'convicted' does not automatically resolve the evidentiary burden question — it merely establishes a conduct-based trigger. The government's forfeiture of any challenge to the clear and convincing evidence standard before both the BIA and the Second Circuit is dispositive here: having accepted that standard in the proceedings below and framed its petition around meeting that burden, the government cannot now relitigate the threshold question of what standard applies. As a pragmatic matter, the case is also a poor vehicle because even a reversal would not resolve removability — the Second Circuit would still need to determine whether trademark counterfeiting constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I), an issue the government has not asked this Court to address. The BIA's own precedent establishing clear and convincing evidence as the default for stripping LPRs of legal protections reflects a reasonable administrative interpretation that serves the workability concerns I find compelling, and I would not disturb the Second Circuit's application of that standard on these facts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) uses 'has committed' rather than 'has been convicted of,' and as this Court recognized in Barton v. Barr, 590 U.S. 222, 232-33 (2020), Congress throughout the INA deliberately distinguishes between conduct-based and conviction-based standards, deploying 'convicted' when it intends a formal judgment requirement. A textualist reading of 'committed' therefore cannot import a conviction prerequisite that Congress chose not to write into the statute. However, the evidentiary burden question is more vexed: the government's forfeiture of the clear-and-convincing standard below is a serious procedural concern, and I would be inclined to remand for the lower courts to address the proper standard in the first instance rather than resolve it here, particularly since the CIMT classification of the underlying offense remains unresolved and may be outcome-determinative regardless of the burden question. The separation of powers dimension also counsels against judicial imposition of an evidentiary standard Congress left unspecified, though the rule of lenity and the canon favoring liberty interests of long-resident aliens would push toward a heightened burden if the Court must supply one.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: As an institutionalist who values judicial restraint and proper preservation of issues, I find the government's failure to challenge the clear and convincing evidence standard before the BIA or the Second Circuit to be a significant procedural barrier — the government accepted that standard below and cannot now seek to relitigate it here. The BIA's own precedent in Rivens, 25 I. & N. Dec. 625, establishing clear and convincing evidence as the default standard for stripping LPRs of their legal protections, represents a reasonable administrative interpretation that the government itself acquiesced to, and this Court should be reluctant to disturb settled agency practice on an unpreserved question. Furthermore, as a practical matter of vehicle selection, even a reversal would not resolve Mr. Lau's removability because the Second Circuit would still need to address whether trademark counterfeiting constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude under INA § 212(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) — a question the government has not asked us to resolve — making this a poor use of the Court's limited docket. The absence of a genuine circuit conflict on the burden-of-proof question, combined with the government's forfeiture, counsels strongly in favor of judicial restraint and denial.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I must begin with the statutory text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C), which Congress enacted in IIRIRA 1996 to replace the Fleuti doctrine with a structured framework for when LPRs are deemed to be seeking admission. While the government's conduct-based reading has textual support — the provision refers to having 'committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2)' without requiring a prior conviction — the government's procedural posture is fatally compromised here. By accepting the clear and convincing evidence standard before both the BIA and the Second Circuit without objection, the government forfeited any challenge to that standard, and basic principles of issue preservation prevent this Court from reaching a question the government declined to contest below. Furthermore, the vehicle problem is genuine: even a reversal on the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) trigger question would not resolve removability, because the moral turpitude characterization of Lau's trademark counterfeiting offense remains unresolved and unasked — meaning any opinion we issue would be advisory as to the ultimate disposition of this case. The BIA's own precedent establishing clear and convincing evidence as the default for stripping LPRs of legal protections reflects a reasonable construction consistent with the heightened stakes for individuals with established lawful status, and the government's failure to challenge that standard below is dispositive.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: As a justice deeply committed to procedural fairness and the rights of individuals facing government power, I find the government's position deeply troubling on multiple grounds. First, the government forfeited its challenge to the clear and convincing evidence standard by accepting it before the BIA and the Second Circuit, and it cannot now seek a lower evidentiary threshold at this stage — basic principles of procedural fairness and issue preservation demand consistency. Second, allowing post-entry conviction evidence to retroactively recharacterize an LPR's prior border crossing as an 'admission' triggering inadmissibility grounds creates a fundamentally unfair retroactive framework that undermines the settled legal status of lawful permanent residents, who have substantial due process interests in their established residency. Third, the case is a poor vehicle regardless, because even if the Court reversed on the burden question, the Second Circuit would still need to resolve whether trademark counterfeiting constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude — an issue the government has not asked this Court to address — meaning the question presented is not outcome-determinative and granting certiorari would be an inefficient use of judicial resources.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the government can treat a lawful permanent resident (LPR) as seeking admission to the United States — and thus subject to inadmissibility grounds — based on a crime committed before re-entry, and what evidentiary burden the government must meet to invoke the exceptions under INA § 1101(a)(13)(C).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) (defining when an LPR is deemed to be seeking admission); INA § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) (inadmissibility for crimes involving moral turpitude); INA § 1182(h) (waiver of inadmissibility); 8 U.S.C. § 1227 (deportability grounds); 28 U.S.C. § 1254(1) (Supreme Court jurisdiction).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Attorney General argues that Muk Choi Lau, an LPR who committed trademark counterfeiting before his last re-entry into the United States, falls within the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) exception, which strips him of LPR protections and renders him subject to inadmissibility grounds as if he were seeking admission for the first time. The government contends that the Second Circuit erred in holding Lau was not removable under 8 U.S.C. § 1227, and that the government properly met its evidentiary burden — including by relying on evidence (the June 24, 2013 conviction) that developed after Lau was paroled into the country following his May 7, 2012 arrest. The government further asserts that a conduct-based admission framework is essential to border integrity and public safety, and that requiring conviction-level proof at the border would undermine Congress's intent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Muk Choi Lau, represented by Skadden Arps, argues that the Second Circuit correctly held he was not removable under 8 U.S.C. § 1227, and that the government failed to meet the clear and convincing evidence standard — the applicable BIA-established default burden — required to strip an LPR of legal protections under § 1101(a)(13)(C). Respondent further contends: (1) the question presented is not outcome-determinative because removability still depends on whether his offense qualifies as a crime involving moral turpitude, an issue the government has not asked the Court to resolve; (2) the government forfeited any challenge to the clear and convincing evidence standard by never contesting it before the BIA or the Second Circuit; (3) there is a circuit split on the burden-of-proof question but the government failed to preserve it, making this a poor vehicle for resolution; and (4) Lau is separately ineligible for a § 212(h) waiver, as found by the immigration judge.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's acknowledgment of the forfeiture problem — coming from a justice otherwise sympathetic to the government's textual reading — actually strengthens my resolve rather than weakening it, because it confirms that even the most persuasive version of the Petitioner's argument cannot overcome the government's litigation conduct below. Justice Barrett's proposed narrow holding — reverse on the statutory interpretation question while leaving the burden and CIMT questions for remand — is intellectually attractive but ultimately fails under my minimalist framework: if the Second Circuit on remand must still resolve both the evidentiary burden question (which the government forfeited) and the CIMT question under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I), then our ruling on 'committed' versus 'convicted' would function as an advisory opinion on a question that cannot be outcome-determinative in this case. Justice Thomas is correct that the forfeiture of the burden question is analytically distinct from the statutory interpretation question, but my minimalist instincts counsel that we should not reach significant questions of immigration law — affecting millions of LPRs — when the vehicle problems are this severe and the government's own litigation conduct forecloses the relief it seeks. As Chief Justice, I would assign a narrow opinion affirming the Second Circuit on forfeiture and vehicle grounds, expressly reserving the 'committed' versus 'convicted' question for a case that properly presents it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh's vehicle concern — that even a correct ruling on 'committed' versus 'convicted' would be non-outcome-determinative given the unresolved CIMT question under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) — is the argument that most genuinely tests my position, and I must engage with it directly. However, this Court regularly resolves antecedent legal questions even when downstream issues remain on remand, and the alternative — allowing the Second Circuit's demonstrably erroneous collapse of 'committed' into 'convicted' to stand because the case presents downstream complications — would permit a clear statutory error to calcify across immigration adjudications affecting millions of LPRs. Justice Kagan's invocation of Chevron deference to the BIA's Rivens standard cannot override Congress's deliberate terminological choice, as Barton v. Barr confirms that 'committed' and 'convicted' are distinct terms of art throughout the INA, and no amount of agency interpretation can render them interchangeable where the text is plain. I maintain my position for a narrow reversal on the statutory interpretation question while remanding without resolving the forfeited evidentiary burden question, consistent with ordinary issue-preservation principles — the vehicle imperfections go to the wisdom of the certiorari grant, not to whether the Second Circuit correctly interpreted the statute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Roberts' forfeiture argument and the vehicle problem remain the most formidable challenges to my position, and I take seriously his point that a reversal would be non-outcome-determinative given the unresolved CIMT question under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I). However, I am persuaded by Justice Gorsuch's narrow remand approach — we can reverse the Second Circuit's erroneous imposition of a conviction-level standard for 'has committed' without resolving the evidentiary burden question the government forfeited, thereby addressing the forfeiture concern while honoring the plain text distinction between 'committed' and 'convicted' that Barton v. Barr confirms is deliberate. Justice Kagan's invocation of Chevron deference to the BIA's Rivens standard is unavailing under my methodology — agency deference cannot override a clear congressional choice to use 'committed' rather than 'convicted,' and the INA's consistent use of both terms as distinct throughout the statute forecloses treating them as interchangeable. The vehicle problem is real but goes to the wisdom of the certiorari grant, not to whether the Second Circuit correctly interpreted the statute — and leaving circuit courts without guidance on a squarely presented statutory question because the case presents downstream complications is precisely the kind of judicial avoidance I find most problematic.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the strongest opposing argument — that Congress's deliberate choice of 'committed' over 'convicted' in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) reflects a conduct-based threshold, consistent with Barton v. Barr's recognition that the INA uses these terms as distinct terms of art. I take that textual argument seriously, but it does not resolve the case in the government's favor for two independent reasons. First, as Justice Kagan correctly identifies, the government forfeited any challenge to the clear-and-convincing evidence standard by accepting it below and arguing it was met — this is not a mere technicality but a foundational principle of issue preservation that prevents the government from reframe the evidentiary question before this Court. Second, even accepting arguendo that 'committed' is conduct-based, the government's framework of paroling Lau into the country and then retroactively recharacterizing his admission status based on a conviction obtained over a year later creates precisely the kind of malleable, unpredictable legal framework that undermines the settled expectations of millions of LPRs — a real-world consequence that Congress did not clearly authorize in IIRIRA's text and that Justice Kavanaugh rightly identifies as a serious workability concern. The vehicle problems Justice Kagan and I have both identified — the unresolved CIMT question under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) — further counsel against this Court issuing what would effectively be an advisory ruling on the admission question.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that the government's forfeiture goes only to the evidentiary burden question and not to the antecedent statutory interpretation question is the most sophisticated challenge to my position, and I want to engage with it directly: even granting that the 'committed' versus 'convicted' question is technically preserved, my pragmatic textualist methodology asks whether resolving that question would actually do useful work in this case, and the answer is no. As I noted in my prior reasoning and as Justice Roberts reinforces, the unresolved CIMT question under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) means that a reversal on the 'committed' question would not be outcome-determinative — the Second Circuit on remand would still need to resolve whether Lau's offense qualifies as a CIMT, and if it does not, the government loses regardless of how we read 'committed.' Justice Gorsuch's response — that circuit conflict on the statutory question justifies correction even in an imperfect vehicle — has genuine force, but I cannot accept that the need to resolve a circuit conflict overrides the basic principle that this Court should not issue rulings that function as advisory opinions on questions that cannot change the outcome below. The combination of the government's affirmative acceptance of the clear-and-convincing standard, the non-outcome-determinative nature of any reversal, and the retroactive recharacterization problem Justice Sotomayor identifies together make this a case where judicial restraint is not avoidance but sound jurisprudence.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press hardest on the vehicle problem — that even a correct ruling on 'committed' versus 'convicted' leaves the CIMT question unresolved, making any reversal non-outcome-determinative and functionally advisory. I take this seriously, but I cannot accept the implication that a circuit court's clear statutory error should go uncorrected simply because downstream questions remain. The Second Circuit's effective collapse of 'committed' into 'convicted' is a legal error that will recur across cases, and Barton v. Barr's recognition of Congress's deliberate terminological choices forecloses the respondent's reading regardless of vehicle imperfections. I maintain my position for a narrow reversal and remand — reversing only on the 'committed' question while explicitly declining to resolve the evidentiary burden issue given the government's forfeiture, and leaving the CIMT question for the Second Circuit — because this disposition respects issue-preservation principles while correcting the statutory error Justice Thomas and Justice Alito correctly identify, and avoids the greater harm of allowing a demonstrably wrong legal standard to calcify in the circuits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that the forfeiture goes only to the evidentiary burden question and not to the antecedent statutory interpretation question is the most intellectually serious challenge to my position, and I acknowledge its force — she is correct that these are analytically separable questions. However, my institutionalist framework leads me to a different conclusion than Justice Barrett's: even accepting that the 'committed' versus 'convicted' question is technically preserved, a reversal on that question would not be outcome-determinative given the unresolved CIMT question under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I), which means we would be issuing what Chief Justice Roberts correctly characterizes as a functional advisory opinion on a significant immigration law question affecting millions of LPRs. Justice Gorsuch's concern that the Second Circuit's error will 'calcify in the circuits' absent correction is legitimate, but my minimalist methodology — which aligns with the Chief Justice's — counsels that the appropriate response to a poor vehicle is to await a better-presented case rather than to issue guidance that cannot actually resolve the dispute before us. The combination of the government's litigation conduct below, the non-outcome-determinative nature of any reversal, and the practical workability concerns Justice Sotomayor identifies about retroactive recharacterization of admission status together reinforce my view that judicial restraint is the appropriate course here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Roberts press the forfeiture argument most forcefully, and I must engage with it directly: the government's acceptance of the clear-and-convincing standard below is a genuine procedural obstacle, but it forecloses only the evidentiary burden question — it does not forfeit the antecedent statutory interpretation question of whether 'committed' in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) requires conduct-based proof rather than a formal conviction, which is the question the Second Circuit actually decided and which is squarely presented here. Justice Kavanaugh's vehicle concern about the unresolved CIMT question is the argument that most genuinely troubles me, because a reversal that does not resolve the underlying case risks functioning as an advisory opinion — but I am persuaded by Justice Thomas's response that this goes to the wisdom of the certiorari grant rather than the merits of the statutory question, and the circuit conflict on 'committed' versus 'convicted' will persist absent this Court's guidance. My proposed disposition — reversing the Second Circuit's effective imposition of a conviction-level standard while explicitly leaving the evidentiary burden question and the CIMT question for resolution on remand — threads the needle between honoring the government's forfeiture and correcting the Second Circuit's textual error, consistent with Barton v. Barr's recognition that 'committed' and 'convicted' are deliberate congressional distinctions throughout the INA. I maintain my position for Petitioner on this narrow statutory interpretation ground, though my confidence remains modest given the legitimate vehicle concerns my colleagues have raised.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the strongest opposing argument — that Congress's deliberate choice of 'committed' over 'convicted' in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) reflects a conduct-based threshold, consistent with Barton v. Even accepting Justice Gorsuch's partial concession that 'committed' is conduct-based, his own reasoning acknowledges the forfeiture problem counsels against resolving the evidentiary burden question in the government's favor, and Justice Kagan correctly notes that the BIA's Rivens standard is entitled to deference as a reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous provision. Most critically, as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kavanaugh both emphasize, allowing the government to retroactively rely on a conviction that postdated Lau's parole into the country to recharacterize his admission status raises profound due process and practical workability concerns that Congress did not clearly authorize — and the unresolved CIMT question under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) makes this a poor vehicle for the broader statutory interpretation question the government seeks to litigate.

John Roberts.reasoning: My minimalist instincts counsel against reaching the broad question presented here, particularly given the significant procedural defects in the government's petition. The government forfeited any challenge to the clear and convincing evidence standard by never contesting it before the BIA or the Second Circuit — indeed, the government itself argued it met that standard, which constitutes a concession that the standard applies. Furthermore, even if I were to reverse on the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) question, the Second Circuit would still need to resolve on remand whether trademark counterfeiting constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude under INA § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I), meaning this Court's intervention would not be outcome-determinative — a factor that weighs heavily against granting certiorari and against the Petitioner on the merits. The institutional legitimacy of the Court is not served by issuing advisory rulings on questions that will not resolve the underlying case, and the absence of a genuine circuit split on the burden-of-proof question — given that the BIA's Rivens standard has been assumed correct by the Second and Fifth Circuits — further undermines the government's case for reversal.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of INA § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) uses the phrase 'has committed an offense' — not 'has been convicted of an offense' — and under ordinary principles of textualism and original public meaning, 'committed' refers to conduct, not a formal judicial determination. Congress's deliberate choice of 'committed' over 'convicted' in this provision, contrasted with other INA provisions that expressly require conviction, reflects a conduct-based threshold. The 1996 IIRIRA legislative history confirms Congress intended to restore meaningful border scrutiny for returning LPRs who engaged in criminal conduct, explicitly overturning the Fleuti doctrine's broad protections and replacing it with a framework that allows immigration officials to act on reliable evidence of criminal conduct at the border. While I have some concern about the evidentiary burden question and the government's forfeiture argument, the core statutory interpretation question — whether 'has committed' requires conviction-level proof — must be resolved in favor of the government's conduct-based reading, as that is what the plain text and original public meaning of the 1996 amendments support.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The statutory text of INA § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) uses the term 'committed' rather than 'convicted,' and as a textualist I must give effect to Congress's deliberate word choice — throughout the INA, Congress consistently uses 'convicted' when it intends a formal judgment of guilt to be required, and 'committed' when conduct alone suffices, as this Court recognized in Barton v. Barr, 590 U.S. 222, 232-33 (2020). Importing a clear-and-convincing evidentiary standard into the border-screening context collapses the structural distinction Congress drew between initial border inspection and full removal adjudication before an immigration judge, effectively rewriting the statute to require conviction-level proof that Congress plainly did not demand. The government's use of post-parole conviction evidence is consistent with the statutory framework because the INA's border-inspection process is designed as a screening mechanism that defers final merits adjudication to removal proceedings, and the Second Circuit's approach would disable parole as a practical tool and force premature merits determinations at ports of entry contrary to congressional design. While I acknowledge the respondent's forfeiture arguments regarding the burden-of-proof standard have some procedural force, the core statutory interpretation question — whether 'committed' is conduct-based — is squarely presented and warrants reversal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: As a pragmatic jurist deeply concerned with the real-world impacts on vulnerable populations, I find that the government's attempt to retroactively strip Mr. Lau of his lawful permanent resident protections under INA § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) raises profound fairness concerns. The BIA itself established clear and convincing evidence as the default standard for invoking § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions — a standard the government never challenged before the BIA or the Second Circuit, thereby forfeiting the issue. Allowing the government to rely on a conviction that post-dated Lau's parole into the country to retroactively justify treating him as an inadmissible alien at the moment of re-entry would undermine the settled expectations of LPRs and create a dangerously malleable framework that could be weaponized against the most vulnerable immigrants. Furthermore, even if the Court were to reverse on the admission question, the Second Circuit would still need to resolve whether trademark counterfeiting constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude under INA § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I), making this a poor vehicle for the broader question the government seeks to litigate.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The government's failure to preserve the burden-of-proof challenge before the BIA or the Second Circuit is a significant procedural obstacle that a pragmatic textualist cannot ignore — the government itself accepted the clear and convincing evidence standard and argued it was met, foreclosing any challenge to that standard now. Under INA § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), the statutory text places the burden on the government to establish that an LPR falls within an exception to the general rule that returning residents are not 'seeking admission,' and the BIA's own precedent in Rivens establishing clear and convincing evidence as the default standard is entitled to deference under Chevron's successor framework as a reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statutory provision. Furthermore, as respondent correctly notes, even a reversal on the admission question would not resolve removability because the Second Circuit would still need to determine whether trademark counterfeiting constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) — making this a poor vehicle for the broader question the government seeks to litigate. The workability concern cuts toward affirming: allowing post-parole conviction evidence to retroactively reframe an LPR's status at the border would create serious administrative and due process complications that Congress did not clearly authorize in the statutory text.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of INA § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) uses 'has committed an offense' rather than 'has been convicted of an offense,' and as this Court recognized in Barton v. Barr, 590 U.S. 222, 232-33 (2020), Congress throughout the INA deliberately distinguishes between 'committed' and 'convicted' as terms of art with distinct legal consequences — a textual distinction I am bound to honor rather than collapse. The conduct-based reading also fits the structural logic Congress enacted: a two-stage framework of border screening followed by full adjudication in removal proceedings, meaning the government need not prove conviction-level facts at the port of entry so long as final removability is adjudicated before an immigration judge under appropriate procedural protections. However, I have serious reservations about the government's forfeiture problem on the evidentiary burden question — if the government never contested the clear-and-convincing standard before the BIA or Second Circuit, ordinary principles of issue preservation counsel strongly against this Court resolving that question in the government's favor, and I would remand for the lower courts to address removability under the correct 'committed' standard without prejudging the burden issue the government failed to preserve.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: As an institutionalist who values both precedent and practical workability, I find the Second Circuit's holding persuasive that the government must meet a clear and convincing evidence standard before stripping an LPR of the substantial protections afforded by § 1101(a)(13)(C). The statutory text of INA § 1101(a)(13)(C) establishes a default presumption that returning LPRs are not seeking admission, and the government's conduct-based parole-then-prosecute framework — relying on a conviction that postdated Lau's re-entry by over a year — strains the statutory text beyond what Congress plausibly intended in IIRIRA. While I take seriously the government's public safety arguments and the congressional intent behind the 1996 reforms to restore meaningful border scrutiny, the government's forfeiture of the burden-of-proof challenge before the BIA and Second Circuit is a significant procedural obstacle that counsels judicial restraint, and the case presents vehicle problems that make it a poor occasion to resolve the circuit split on evidentiary standards. The practical workability concerns cut both ways here — a rule permitting indefinite post-entry evidence gathering to retroactively recharacterize an LPR's admission status would create significant uncertainty for the millions of lawful permanent residents who rely on settled expectations about their legal status.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of INA § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) uses the word 'committed' rather than 'convicted,' and as the government correctly notes — consistent with this Court's recognition in Barton v. Barr, 590 U.S. 222, 232-33 (2020) — Congress throughout the INA deliberately distinguishes conduct-based and conviction-based triggers, suggesting the original public meaning of 'committed' does not require a formal judgment of guilt at the time of border inspection. The statutory architecture of IIRAIRA supports a conduct-based screening framework at ports of entry, with full adjudication reserved for removal proceedings before an immigration judge, meaning the Second Circuit erred in effectively importing a conviction-level proof requirement into the border-screening context. However, my confidence is tempered by the respondent's serious vehicle concerns: the government's apparent forfeiture of any challenge to the clear-and-convincing evidence standard before the BIA and Second Circuit is a significant procedural obstacle, and the question of whether Lau's offense constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) remains unresolved, meaning a reversal may not be outcome-determinative on remand. I would vote to reverse the Second Circuit's effective imposition of a conviction-level standard, while acknowledging that the forfeiture issue and the unresolved CIMT question may counsel a narrow holding or a remand with instructions rather than a full resolution of the evidentiary burden question.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: As a progressive pragmatist with deep concern for procedural fairness and the practical consequences of stripping lawful permanent residents of their legal protections, I find the government's position deeply problematic on multiple grounds. First, the government forfeited any challenge to the clear and convincing evidence standard by never contesting it before the BIA or the Second Circuit, and basic principles of issue preservation preclude the government from raising this argument for the first time before this Court. Dec. 625, establishes clear and convincing evidence as the default standard for invoking § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions — a standard the government itself accepted below — and allowing the government to retroactively rely on a conviction that postdated Lau's parole into the country raises serious due process concerns about the fairness of the admission determination. Third, as a former public defender, I am acutely aware that permitting the government to treat LPRs as first-time admission seekers based on conduct-level evidence, without a robust evidentiary burden, creates a framework ripe for abuse that disproportionately harms communities of color and undermines the settled expectations of millions of lawful permanent residents who have built their lives in this country.
